certainty_reasoning: Cook states plainly that Ives shared his bed with James Goddard ('Kit') at the Albany, which is more explicit than the household-membership evidence behind the Bloodworth record. It stays 'alleged' on the single-source rule: Cook (2003) is the only work read that attests it, and bed-sharing in a shared bachelor household is not by itself a statement of sexual relations. CORROBORATION: Cook returns to this household at much greater length in Queer Domesticities (2014), where he states that the Adelaide Road relationships 'possibly started sexually' before settling into something platonic, with bed-sharing continuing throughout. Cook's account of the Ives household is drawn from Ives's own 122-volume diary and his endnotes cite it by volume and date; the tier follows whose testimony underlies the claim, not whether our record happens to carry a direct quotation rather than the historian's summary of the same diary.

date_label: Albany period, from 1894; Kit later at Adelaide Road
summary: One of the two young men of George Ives's Albany household - the circle of working-class and dependent young men he called his 'children' - with whom Cook records Ives sharing his bed.

disputed.claim: That the bed-sharing recorded by Cook was a sexual or romantic relationship.
disputed.asserted_by: Cook, London and the Culture of Homosexuality (2003), p. 146, as read by the editor
disputed.disputed_by: Single-source and uncorroborated in the works read; Cook himself does not characterize it as sexual
disputed.grounds: Cook's sentence attests shared sleeping arrangements in Ives's household, not sexual relations; Ives's diaries (Harry Ransom Center) and Kaplan (2005) are the verification targets.

sources.quote: Using pet names for his co-residents, he wrote: 'Kit has been with me some 35 years. His wife over 20. Pug 9 or 10. [.] and the 2 Kit girls all their lives'. 'Kit' (James Goddard) had been a servant at the Ives' family seat in Hampshire and then moved with George to London.
sources.context: Cook's opening to the Ives chapter, quoting the roll call Ives made in his diary in 1917 of his 'family' home at Adelaide Road; Cook's endnote 1 cites Diary vol. 70, 21 May 1917, p. 118. The '[.]' is Cook's own elision inside Ives's sentence.
sources.supports: Goddard in Ives's own words, and the plainest first-hand statement of what this bond was: Ives counts Kit first in the roll call of his household and measures the attachment in decades - 'some 35 years' by 1917, which reaches back past the Albany to Ives's father's estate in Hampshire. It is a claim of family rather than of service or of sex; Cook notes on the same page that Ives called the group 'my little circle in the world'. Ives's diary, vol. 70, 21 May 1917, as quoted by Cook.
sources.provenance: PDF pp. 106-107 (printed folios 95 and 96 confirmed on the rendered pages; the quotation runs across the page break, breaking at 'has been with me some / 35 years').

sources.quote: Ives shared his new home, and sometimes his bed, with James Goddard (Kit), the son of one of his father's employees, and Harold Holt (Cubby), his grandmother's former secretary.
sources.context: Cook, on Ives's household at E4 the Albany
sources.supports: Bed-sharing household intimacy at the Albany, in Cook's own words

sources.quote: Kit brought his wife and children to live there for a while, and in 1909, Harold Bloodworth, a teenage footballer, moved in and stayed until Ives' death in 1950.
sources.context: Cook on Ives's move to Adelaide Road, Primrose Hill, in 1905 - the household intimacy outlasting Kit Goddard's marriage.
sources.supports: Cook records that Kit later brought his wife and children to live at Adelaide Road for a time - the household intimacy outlasting his marriage. Transcription pending.

sources.quote: Though Ives' relationships with the other men at Adelaide Road possibly started sexually, they seem quickly to have become platonic - even though he continued to sleep with them from time to time.
sources.context: Cook's summary characterization of the Adelaide Road household relationships
sources.supports: Cook's own careful reading: a possible sexual beginning, a platonic settling, continued bed-sharing throughout.

sources.quote: The men thus shifted from (possible) lovers to sons and, in bed, to comrades.
sources.context: Cook, immediately after quoting Ives's diary on sleeping beside Pug and Cubby

sources.quote: The Albany sets (as the chambers are called) were part of a recognisable bachelor tradition and were spacious, self-contained, and with room for a live-in servant - in Ives' case James Goddard/Kit (though he seems also to have shared Ives' bed).
sources.context: Cook, on the Albany chambers and their live-in servant provision
sources.supports: A second statement by Cook, in his 2014 book, of the Goddard bed-sharing - located specifically at the Albany and framed as an aside qualifying Goddard's servant role. Corroborates the Cook 2003 p. 146 sentence already in this record, but from the same author, so it does not supply independent attestation. Cook hedges: 'seems also to have'.
sources.provenance: PDF pp. 109-110 (printed folios 98 and 99 confirmed on the rendered pages; the sentence runs across the page break).

sources.quote: James and Sylvie Goddard remained with Ives until their deaths; their daughters until the early 1940s.
sources.context: Cook, on the duration of the Goddards' residence at Adelaide Road
sources.supports: Duration: the Goddard co-residence with Ives lasted until the Goddards' deaths - the longest attachment in the household apart from Bloodworth's. Also dates the daughters' departure to the early 1940s.
